analysis.one_liner: Bars permits for sulfide mining near the Great Lakes unless miners prove no acid drainage.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a committee vote or a floor vote; it died at the end of the 110th Congress with no cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would change the Clean Water Act so that no permit could be issued for mine discharge from a sulfide ore body within 20 miles of any Great Lake unless the mining company first proves the mine will not cause acid mine drainage into the Lakes. Sulfide ores, common in copper and nickel mining, react with air and water to form sulfuric acid that can leach heavy metals into waterways. The bill was introduced by Rep. Bart Stupak in March 2007, sent to the House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee, then to its water subcommittee, and never advanced.
analysis.who_benefits: The roughly 40 million people whose drinking water and livelihoods depend on the Great Lakes, plus tourism and fishing interests in the basin, would gain protection against acid mine drainage from sulfide mining operations near the Lakes.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Great Lakes region residents and fisheries

how_it_helps.text: It shifts the burden of proof: within 20 miles of a Great Lake, a mining company would have to demonstrate, to the regulator's satisfaction, that its sulfide mine will not produce acid mine drainage into the Lakes before any discharge permit can be issued [S2][S3].

Acid mine drainage forms when sulfide minerals in ore are exposed to air and water, producing sulfuric acid that can carry dissolved metals into rivers and lakes; the bill's stated purpose is to protect Great Lakes water quality from this harm [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Mining companies hoping to dig copper, nickel, or other metals from sulfide deposits near the Great Lakes would bear the cost of proving their mines safe before permits are issued, and some projects near the Lakes could become uneconomical or impossible to permit.
analysis.who_pays_short: Mining companies near the Great Lakes

drawbacks.text: The bar is high and somewhat open-ended: an applicant must prove a negative — that a mine over the life of its operation will never produce acid drainage — which regulators may treat as effectively impossible to satisfy, blocking mining projects outright rather than managing them with safeguards [S2][S3].

A 20-mile zone around the Lakes reaches well inland, so the restriction would cover mining areas beyond the shoreline and could limit jobs and royalties in rural mining communities that argue modern engineering can control drainage [S2][S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The protection addresses a genuine, hard-to-reverse hazard: once acid mine drainage starts contaminating a lake system holding a fifth of the world's fresh surface water, cleanup is extremely difficult. The cost falls on a small number of potential mining projects and the local jobs they might create. The main design criticism is that the proof standard is strict enough that it functions close to a ban near the Lakes, which supporters would call the point and critics would call overbroad.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Transportation and Infrastructure Committee's water subcommittee, no hearing or vote was ever scheduled, and it expired when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Bart Stupak introduced the bill on March 29, 2007; it was referred the same day to the House Committee on Transportation and Infrastructure [S5].
The next day it was referred to the Subcommittee on Water Resources and Environment, and no further action appears in the record for the rest of the 110th Congress [S5].
The bill had no cosponsors, and it never received a committee vote, a floor vote, or a companion Senate action [S4][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Mining companies interested in sulfide ore deposits within 20 miles of the Great Lakes are better off, since the burden-of-proof permit requirement they would have faced never became law.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Would-be sulfide miners near the Lakes

for.name: Rep. Bart Stupak
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to require proof of no acid mine drainage before permits for sulfide mining near the Great Lakes

against.name: Rep. James Oberstar
against.role: Chair, House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a committee markup or vote on the bill after it was referred to his committee

sides.party_line_note: There were no votes and no cosponsors, so the record shows only a single Democratic sponsor and no identifiable opposition blocs.

industries.note: The bill would have made sulfide mining within 20 miles of the Great Lakes much harder to permit by requiring proof of no acid drainage before any discharge permit. Its interest in operating without that burden runs against the region's interest in clean water, since sulfide mines are the source of the acid drainage the bill targets.
